settings.heading: Emma Addison came south in 1908 with a sewing machine and a letter of introduction. The letter was never needed.
settings.body:
She took a room above a tannery in Saint-Côme-d'Olt and began making riding coats for the women of the valley — garments meant to be worn in weather, mended, and handed on. Four generations later we work in the same building, from the same principle: make a small number of things properly, name the people who made them, and repair them for as long as they are worn.

We show twice a year and never discount. What does not sell returns to the archive, where it is often better than what replaced it.
Emma Addison rents a room above a tannery in Saint-Côme-d'Olt and makes riding coats to order for the women of the valley.
The maison buys the building on rue des Tanneurs, where the workroom, the archive and the cutting table still stand today.
A long correspondence with a Lancashire mill produces the dry-waxed cotton we still use, unchanged, for our outerwear.
Sylvie Fabre joins as an apprentice cutter. She has cut every coat the house has made since 2003.
We begin re-waxing and mending any Addison Emma garment free of charge, whatever its age or owner.
